Holy jeez that's a lot of growing. I'm likely going to pick up 3+ acres in the upper midwest and want to do some of this. Probably corn, potatoes, onions, peppers, the predictable stuff. I'm sure I can research how to grow that stuff, but I'm probably getting this place when fall is kicking in. Wonder if you have any tips to prepare some of the landscape (probably drawing troughs and fertilizing I'm thinking.)

I would definitely recommend a soil analysis when you get there. My county agriculture extension office has litle kits where you send them a box of dirt, and they will test it for free. That will tell you what your soil has, and what its lacking. I found out that out of the N-P-K rating thingie, i was lacking in N and K, but had a large overabundance of P. That gave me an idea of what fertilizer to use. If you go into it not knowing, you can still grow veggies, but obv not optimal for their growth. Im still learning, and mine isnt perfect, but I went organic (fertilizer-wise) this year, and my plants (especially the tomatoes) are happier and sturdier than they have ever been. My corn, on the other hand, is more stunted than its ever been. Havent figured that out yet, unless i wasnt feeding them enough nitrogen, as they are heavy feeders.

If you are getting it in the fall, you are at the prime time to add soil amendments. Till in some compost if you can get your hands on it, or some horse shit or something. Craigslist is a good place to find both. This particular sub is all about using organic things, as conventional fertilizers supposedly rob the soil of nutrients over the long run. Here, we are trying to build our soil, and turn it into the "black gold" you would find on the floor of the forest, or what potting soil looks like in the bag.

I used a tractor to work my land. First we used a plow to turn the grass under. Then we used a disc to chop up the larger lumps. Then we used a tine tiller on the back of the tractor to further remove some of the grass clumps. Last, we made rows. Not sure what that implement is called, but it looks almost like a plow, but instead of blades that only curve one way, they are like spikes and have curve on both sides.

If you dont have all that shit, try Double Digging. That whole self-teaching course is very good, give it a read. I am trying to work my way towards not having to disturb the soil after the first few years. Not sure if I will keep the row/trough setup, or if i will turn my garden into more of a flat bed. I also posted elsewhere (i think it was in one of my older update threads) about this person who grew corn weed free, using a drip irrigation hose and in a raised bed. I know the blog was called "an oregon cottage" if you wanna search for it. Thats a good one to read, and you should be able to apply the principles towards an entire garden. Once you build your soil to satisfactory awesomeness, you shouldnt have to fertilize much, if at all.

Cover crops are also a good thing to enrich your soil. Legumes like peas and clover add nitrogen to your soil, they catch it from the air and use little bacterial nodules to add it back to the soil (i bought crimson clover, but will prob get dutch clover next year).

What i have not figured out yet, is the order of which to do things. This sub's mod @middle_path recommends plant the cover crops in the fall, and let the winter kill them, and then work them into the soil the next spring. It seems that adding organic matter is always a good thing with this growing method. I also started a thread in this sub, called "how to prepare for next year?" that shouldl have a bit of good info that would help you prepare your plot in the fall. Right now im rassling with the order to do things, as i want to work in some horseshit this fall, but also want to do the clover. The horseshit would be too "hot" and needs to overwinter to mellow out. But the legumes need time to do their thing as well. Iunno.
